`gtfs-via-duckdb` is a fork of and the spiritual successor to `gtfs-via-postgres`, importing GTFS into a *DuckDB* database file. The two have the same features, shortcomings and conceptual design (runtime access to the GTFS happens using SQL only).

`gtfs-via-duckdb`'s usage in production systems is much less complex: `duckdb-gtfs-importer` can enable the *robustness* and *atomicity* goals explained in `postgis-gtfs-importer`'s readme with a much simpler design (>1 DB files, symlink to the latest).

Because DuckDB tends to be more efficient than PostgreSQL, with the mostly OLAP-like queries run for GTFS analysis, so `gtfs-via-duckdb` imports datasets faster and queries for common use cases usually run faster.

Stream loader is a collection of libraries providing means to load data from Kafka into arbitrary storages such as Iceberg, HDFS, S3, ClickHouse or Vertica using exactly-once semantics. Users can easily implement various highly customized loaders by combining out of the box components for record formatting and encoding, data storage, stream grouping and so on, implementing their own or extending the existing ones, if needed.

For further complete examples you can explore the loaders used for integration testing, a reference loader for every supported storage is available. For more details about implementing custom loaders refer to the API reference.

An alternative approach is to store data in a two-phase commit, which is done in the HDFS and S3 storage implementations. The _prepare_ step consists of staging a file (uploading to a temporary location in HDFS or starting a multi-part upload in S3) and committing new offsets with the staging information to the Kafka offset commit metadata while retaining the original offsets. The _commit_ step stores the staged file (moves it to the final destination in HDFS or completes the multi-part upload in S3) and commits the new offsets to Kafka, at the same time clearing the staging metadata. In this approach the transaction would be rolled back if the loader crashes before completing the staging phase, or replayed if it crashed after staging.

Stream loader comes bundled with builders for common file formats and macro based encoder derivations that implement case class serialization to CSV, parquet, native Vertica and row binary ClickHouse file formats. These auto derived encoders provide performance equivalent to hand-written code, as they generate straightforward JVM code with little to none object allocation.

- **Kafka Connect**: conceptually the stream loader library is an alternative to the Sink part of the Connect framework. The advantage of Kafka Connect is the enormous ecosystem around it with tons of available sinks to chose from, some of which also provide exactly-once semantics. The main disadvantage (for some, at least) is the need to maintain a cluster of workers. Deployment is also problematic and requires an ad-hoc flow. For a more detailed discussion see KIP-304.
In contrast stream loader is a library meaning that you can use existing orchestrators such as Kubernetes to deploy and run your loaders.

- **Built-in database Kafka ingesters**: some databases such as Vertica and ClickHouse support direct data ingestion from Kafka. The main disadvantage with this approach is the coupling of data processing to the database which can have a performance impact. These mechanisms usually also provide limited options for parsing and transforming the data that is being loaded. On the other hand, using a built-in ingest mechanism can be very easy to configure and deploy for simple data flows.

zeromem: tokenless memory system for Hermes Agent
Memory for Hermes Agent. Every message stays word for word in one SQLite file on your machine. Storing and searching cost zero tokens, and your model only pays to read what comes back.
zeromem is a Rust implementation of Zero-Mem by Xiao et al. (paper, official code).
Messages are saved word for word, indexed three ways and searched on your machine with no LLM calls. Search returns the exact turn. Tokens are only spent when your model reads the result.
Paper to code map and deviations

Pure-Go port of Yjs, the CRDT framework for collaborative applications, listed on the ports page of the Yjs documentation.

Ygo speaks the **Yjs V1 and V2 wire formats** byte for byte, apart from whole-number floats set from Go and a lone surrogate in a V1 embed or format value (see Strings and values). The encoding is verified in both directions through **691 cross-language fixture scenarios** generated from `yjs@13.6.33`. The bundled WebSocket server speaks the `y-websocket` protocol: JavaScript clients using `y-websocket` connect to it directly, and the Go client connects to the reference `y-websocket` server. Since 1.37.0 the server also serves `@hocuspocus/provider` 2.15, 3.4 and 4.8, and the Go client connects to Hocuspocus servers of those versions (see Hocuspocus setup). No CGO; `gomobile bind` produces an Android AAR (built in CI) and an iOS xcframework (built by hand).

- **Byte-level wire compatibility, verified in both directions.** 691 cross-language fixture scenarios (generated from `yjs@13.6.33`) cover the V1 and V2 update formats, snapshots, subdocuments, undo, observers, relative positions, GC, awareness, the sync protocol, and the Any values JavaScript has and Go does not (undefined, BigInt, -0), JS to Go and Go to JS, plus 56 lib0 primitive vectors. The suite runs in CI on every push to `main` and every pull request, so a regression in either direction fails the build. The exceptions are the Any values listed under Strings and values.

- **Pure Go, no CGO.** The CRDT core, the sync client and the server compile with `CGO_ENABLED=0` for all 47 targets in `go tool dist list`, `js/wasm` and `wasip1/wasm` included. The core module needs Go 1.23. The SQLite-backed store in `persist/sqlite`, and with it `yserve` and the mobile SDK, is a module of its own that needs Go 1.26, and builds only where `modernc.org/sqlite` does: not on wasm, AIX, DragonFly, illumos, Plan 9, Solaris, MIPS or big-endian ppc64 Linux, NetBSD other than amd64, or OpenBSD other than amd64 and arm64. Elsewhere, supply your own `persist.Store` (it is a seven-method interface). `gomobile bind` produces an Android AAR (built in CI on every push to `main` and every pull request) and an iOS xcframework (built by hand on 2026-11-10) carrying a full mobile SDK: editable Text / Map, undo, cursors, and a built-in background sync client (WebSocket + reconnect), so a Swift / Kotlin app only renders UI. No V8, no embedded JavaScript engine, no Rust FFI bridge.

- **Embeddable sync client, offline-first.** The `client` package is a Go-native `y-websocket` provider, and with `Options.Hocuspocus` a Hocuspocus one: handshake, incremental updates, awareness, reconnect with backoff, and a liveness check that redials a connection which went silent. With a `LocalStore` it persists the document to disk (pure-Go SQLite), loads it before any network so the app works offline, and syncs edits made offline up on reconnect. The building block for bots, CLI tools, server-side agents, and the mobile SDK (`EnableOfflineStore`).

- **Ready-to-run server: yserve.** A self-hosted Yjs server in one binary, with no Node and no Redis. `y-websocket` clients connect unchanged (CI runs y-websocket 2.1 and 3.1 against it), and SQLite persistence and periodic document versioning are built in. The document is the URL path, slashes included; behind a proxy that keeps a path prefix, pass it as `-path-prefix`. It also embeds as a plain `http.Handler` inside an existing Go backend.

- **Scales horizontally, as a library.** Several instances of the `server` package behind a load balancer converge on the same document through a pluggable backplane: edits and live cursors both cross instances, so two users on different servers collaborate as if on one. An in-process hub ships in the core; an opt-in NATS adapter (a separate module, so NATS stays out of the core's dependencies) spans machines, with a JetStream mode that resumes delivery across a broker reconnect or restart. Clustered instances share one `Store` and run the same ygo version. The `yserve` binary has no backplane option.

- **Federated transport over Matrix.** An opt-in Matrix transport (a separate module, so mautrix stays out of a build that only wants the CRDT) turns an ordinary unencrypted Matrix room into the sync channel: peers publish updates as `dev.ygo.update` room events and merge what they read back, with no ygo server involved. A room is an append-only log with no ordering or exactly-once guarantee, which is exactly what Yjs updates tolerate. Room content is treated as untrusted — validated on both sides, decoded one event at a time so one bad event cannot break a whole page, encrypted rooms refused rather than silently written in the clear — though, as the module README spells out, Yjs updates do not authenticate deletes, so room membership is write access to the document. Exercised in CI against a real Dendrite on every push to `main` and every pull request. Its limits are documented rather than papered over.
